claim: Hydra vulgaris is an emerging model organism for neuroscience due to its small size, transparency, genetic tractability, and regenerative nervous system.
source: Hydra vulgaris is an emerging model organism for neuroscience due to its small size, transparency, genetic tractability, and regenerative nervous system
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that describes the properties of Hydra vulgaris as a model organism.

claim: Mechanical stimuli cause Hydra to contract.
source: Mechanical stimuli cause animals to contract
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The mechanosensory response in Hydra relies on at least two distinct networks of neurons in the oral and aboral regions of the animal.
source: we find this response relies on at least two distinct networks of neurons in the oral and aboral regions of the animal
evidence: This claim is supported by resection experiments and calcium imaging data showing different neural networks.

claim: Different activity patterns arise in oral and aboral neural networks depending on whether the animal is contracting spontaneously or in response to mechanical stimulation.
source: Different activity patterns arise in these networks depending on whether the animal is contracting spontaneously or contracting in response to mechanical stimulation
evidence: This is supported by single-neuron tracking and correlation analysis showing distinct patterns for spontaneous vs. stimulated contractions.

claim: Hydra has a diffuse nervous system composed of two networks, one embedded in the endoderm and another in the ectoderm.
source: This radially symmetric freshwater cnidarian has a nervous system composed of two diffuse networks of neurons, one embedded in the endoderm and another embedded in the ectoderm (Burnett and Diehl, 1964; Lfntz and Barrnett, 1965)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Hydra can completely recover from significant neuronal loss to regain normal contractile behavior in as little as ~48 hr.
source: Hydra can completely recover from a significant neuronal loss to regain normal contractile behavior in as little as ~48 hr (Itayama and Sawada, 1995; Soriano et al., 2009; Gierer et al., 1972)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Regions with increased neuron density resembling nerve rings in Hydra have comparatively lower neuronal turnover.
source: regions with increased neuron density resembling nerve rings have a comparatively lower neuronal turnover (Figure 1a; Bode et al., 1973; Epp and Tardent, 1978; Koizumi et al., 1992; Hufnagel and Kass-Simon, 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the text with supporting citations and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: One nerve ring region is in the oral end in the apex above the ring of tentacles (hypostomal nerve ring).
source: One of these regions is in the oral end in the apex above the ring of tentacles ('hypostomal nerve ring')
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about Hydra anatomy.

claim: Another nerve ring region is in the aboral end in the foot (peduncle nerve ring).
source: another is in the aboral end in the foot ('peduncle nerve ring') (Figure 1a)
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about Hydra anatomy with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: There is no overlap in the neuronal cell types that make up the hypostomal and peduncle nerve rings.
source: This existing molecular and spatial map of the nervous system suggests that there is no overlap in the neuronal cell types that make up the hypostomal and peduncle nerve rings
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA sequencing data from Siebert et al., 2019.

claim: The distribution of neuronal cell types varies along the length of the Hydra body.
source: the distribution of the cell types varies along the length of the body (Figure 1b)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b based on single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing has provided a complete molecular and spatial map of the Hydra nervous system.
source: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing has provided a complete molecular and spatial map of the Hydra nervous system, including identification of unique cell-type-specific biomarkers to generate new transgenic models (Siebert et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Siebert et al., 2019.

claim: The microfluidic system delivers a local mechanical stimulus with most of the mechanical force localized to a radius of approximately 250 µm around the microfluidic valve.
source: Experiments showed that this stimulation paradigm delivered a local mechanical stimulation with most of the mechanical force localized to a radius of approximately 250 µm around the microfluidic valve
evidence: This is supported by cellular displacement measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neurons more than 750 µm from the microfluidic valve center showed a negligible displacement of less than 5 µm.
source: Neurons more than 750 µm from the microfluidic valve center showed a negligible displacement of less than 5 µm (95% CI lower bound = 5.8 µm), which is ~550% less than the displacement of neurons bordering the valve
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of neuronal displacement during mechanical stimulation.

claim: Mechanical stimuli generated bright calcium signals from a small number of neurons in the hypostome and body column and a striking co-activation of many neurons in the ectodermal peduncle nerve ring.
source: When we delivered mechanical stimuli, we found bright calcium signals generated by a small number of neurons in the hypostome and body column and a striking co-activation of many neurons in the ectodermal peduncle nerve ring (Figure 2b, Videos 2 and 3)
evidence: This is observed through calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2b and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: The peduncle nerve ring activity appeared as either a single bright calcium spike (contraction pulse) or a volley of bright calcium spikes (contraction burst).
source: This nerve ring activity appeared as either a single bright calcium spike (or 'contraction pulse') or a volley of bright calcium spikes (or 'contraction burst')
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging observations.

claim: The calcium-sensitive fluorescence averaged over a region of interest surrounding the peduncle faithfully represented the contraction pulses and bursts measured from individual neurons.
source: We also found that the calcium-sensitive fluorescence averaged over a region of interest (ROI) surrounding the peduncle faithfully represented the contraction pulses and bursts measured from individual neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 comparing large ROI and individual neuron traces.

claim: Single-neuron calcium dynamics from the peduncle nerve ring showed extremely high correlated activity.
source: When we analyzed single-neuron calcium dynamics from this peduncle nerve ring, we found extremely high correlated activity as previously reported for contractions pulses and bursts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Dupre and Yuste, 2017; Badhiwala et al., 2018)
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-neuron calcium traces with supporting citations.

claim: Hydra were five times more likely to contract within 1 s of receiving a strong mechanical stimulus (20 or 25 psi) than during a random 1 s interval without a stimulus.
source: Hydra were five times more likely to contract within 1 s of receiving a strong mechanical stimulus than during a random 1 s interval without a stimulus (stimulus valve pressure 20 and 25 psi; response probability = 0.60 ± 0.06 and 0.77 ± 0.08, mean ± SEM, respectively; no stimulus valve pressure = 0 psi; response probability = 0.11 ± 0.01, mean ± SEM; Figure 2e, h)
evidence: This is quantified from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2e, h.

claim: During mild stimuli (10 and 15 psi), there was a slight increase (~2×) in response probability above spontaneous activity, although this increase was not statistically significant.
source: During mild stimuli, there was a slight increase (~2×) in response probability above the spontaneous activity, although this increase was not statistically significant compared to spontaneous contraction bursts or pulses (valve pressure 10 and 15 psi; response probability = 0.23 ± 0.01 and 0.24 ± 0.03, mean ± SEM, respectively; Figure 2e, h)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of response probabilities at different stimulus intensities.

claim: Hydra did not respond to a weak mechanical stimulus corresponding to a valve pressure of 5 psi.
source: We found that Hydra did not respond to a weak mechanical stimulus that corresponded to a valve pressure of 5 psi (response probability = 0.09 ± 0.02, mean ± SEM; Figure 2e, h)
evidence: This is based on response probability measurements shown in Figure 2e, h.

claim: Single contraction pulses were more frequent when mechanical stimulation was repeated every 31 s for 1 hr.
source: Further analysis of the calcium activity pattern revealed that the single contraction pulses (calcium spikes in the peduncle neurons) were more frequent when we repeated mechanical stimulation every 31 s for 1 hr
evidence: This is based on analysis of calcium activity patterns during repeated stimulation.

claim: When Hydra were stimulated with strong mechanical stimuli, the frequency of contractions nearly matched the 31 s between stimuli.
source: when we stimulated Hydra with a strong mechanical stimuli, we found that the frequency nearly matched the 31 s between stimuli (Interval between spontaneous contraction bursts or pulses = 72.98 s ± 4.58, mean ± SEM; 66.68 ± 5.73 s median ± SE; Interval between stimulated contraction bursts or pulses = 20 psi, 38.28 ± 1.77 s, mean ± SEM; 31.14 ± 2.21 s, median ± SE; 25 psi, 32.20 ± 1.04 s, mean ± SEM; 31.14 ± 1.30 s, median ± SE; Figure 2f, h)
evidence: This is quantified from analysis of inter-contraction intervals shown in Figure 2f, h.

claim: Stimulated calcium spikes were roughly three times more likely to be single contraction pulses compared to spontaneous calcium spikes.
source: While the majority of spontaneous calcium spikes formed bursts, stimulated calcium spikes were roughly three times more likely to be a single contraction pulses (percentage of spontaneous spiking activity that is a single contraction pulse = 0 psi, 16.87 ± 5.38% mean ± SEM; percentage of stimulated spiking activity that is a single contraction pulse = 20 psi, 56.84 ± 2.48%; 25 psi, 62.50 ± 5.23%, mean ± SEM; Figure 2g, h)
evidence: This is quantified from analysis of contraction patterns shown in Figure 2g, h.

claim: The aboral end of Hydra is less sensitive to mechanical stimulation than the center of the body.
source: we found the aboral end of Hydra to be less sensitive than the center of the body (aboral region response probability = 0.1 ± 0.025; mid-body region response probability = 0.42 ± 0.025; mean ± SEM; p<0.01; Figure 2—figure supplement 7a)
evidence: This is based on experiments stimulating different body regions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7a.

claim: The difference in sensitivity along the Hydra body was not an artifact due to differently sized Hydra experiencing different pressures from the microfluidic valves.
source: Furthermore, we found that the difference in sensitivity along the body was not an artifact due to differently sized Hydra experiencing different pressures from the microfluidic valves. We observed no statistically significant trend between animal size and response probability (Figure 2—figure supplement 7c)
evidence: This is based on analysis of response probability vs. body size shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7c.

claim: The same motor program was initiated regardless of where on the body the animal was touched.
source: we observed that the same motor program was initiated regardless of where on the body the animal was touched
evidence: This is based on observations from stimulation experiments at different body locations.

claim: The response probability depended on where along the oral and aboral axis the mechanical stimulus was delivered.
source: The only difference we observed was the fact that the response probability depended on where along the oral and aboral axis we delivered the mechanical stimulus
evidence: This is based on experiments showing different response probabilities at different body locations.

claim: The mechanosensory response is mediated by electrically coupled cells rather than passive calcium diffusion through epithelial cells.
source: Based on the latency of the mechanosensory response, we hypothesized that sensorimotor information is transmitted by electrical activity in the Hydra and not by passive calcium diffusion through epithelial cells
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by response time measurements and comparison with theoretical calcium diffusion times.

claim: Aneural Hydra are capable of aversive contractile response to touch, but their responses are slow and require strong mechanical stimulus.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the fact that aneural Hydra, which no longer spontaneously contract in the absence of stimuli, are capable of aversive contractile response to touch; however, their responses are slow and require strong mechanical stimulus (Campbell et al., 1976; Takaku et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Fast propagation of calcium activity was observed throughout the entire endoderm during mechanical stimulation.
source: However, this was not the case; we observed fast propagation of calcium activity throughout the entire endoderm
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging of endodermal epitheliomuscular cells.

claim: Changes in neural activity correlated with observed changes in epithelial muscle cells with increasing stimulus intensity.
source: Imaging calcium activity in the peduncle neurons showed that changes in neural activity correlated with the observed changes in epithelial muscle cells with increasing stimulus intensity (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is shown through simultaneous imaging of neurons and muscles at different stimulus intensities.

claim: The 0.5 s average response time could not be explained by calcium diffusion alone, which would take ~100 s to travel the average distance of ~0.5–1 mm.
source: Although Hydra's behavioral responses are slow compared to other invertebrates, the 0.5 s average response time in our data could not be explained by calcium diffusion alone, which would take ~100 s to travel the average distance of ~0.5–1 mm between the stimulation site and the peduncle or hypostome (Figure 2—figure supplement 8a)
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations of calcium diffusion shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8a.

claim: Calcium signals from peduncle neurons or endodermal muscles start increasing within ~0.1–0.2 s following stimulation onset, reaching peak fluorescence at ~0.5–0.6 s regardless of stimulus intensity.
source: Our data show that the calcium signals from the peduncle neurons or endodermal muscles start increasing within ~0.1–0.2 s following stimulation onset, reaching peak fluorescence at ~0.5–0.6 s regardless of the stimulus intensity (Figure 2—figure supplement 8b–e)
evidence: This is based on analysis of calcium response kinetics shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8b–e.

claim: The recovery time of 6–12 hr after resection is long enough to allow wounds to close and initial molecular events of regeneration to start, but not long enough for the animal to regenerate lost neurons.
source: This period is long enough to allow the wounds to close, the molecular response to injury to be completed (Cazet and Juliano, 2020; Tursch et al., 2020), and the initial molecular events of regeneration to start; but it is not long enough for the animal to regenerate lost neurons, which takes approximately 30–72 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Itayama and Sawada, 1995; Pierobon, 2015; Bode, 2003; Goel et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 6–12 hr after resection, animals showed loss of specific neuronal cell types as measured by expression levels of subtype-specific neuronal markers via qPCR.
source: We confirmed that 6–12 hr after resection the animals indeed showed loss of specific neuronal cell types by measuring the expression levels of subtype-specific neuronal markers via qPCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The aboral nerve ring is not required to regulate spontaneous contraction bursts or pulses or mechanosensory responses.
source: our experiments with 'footless' animals showed that the aboral nerve ring was not required to regulate spontaneous contraction bursts or pulses or mechanosensory responses
evidence: This is based on experiments with footless Hydra showing no significant difference in response compared to whole animals.

claim: The increase in contraction burst or pulse activity with stimuli in 'footless' individuals was similar to the increase observed in whole individuals.
source: After we removed the peduncle network in Hydra, we found that the increase in contraction burst or pulse activity with stimuli (or mechanosensory response) in 'footless' individuals was similar to the increase in activity observed in whole individuals ('footless' N = 8 animals stimulated 20 min, Cohen's d = 1.89, Cliff's delta = 0.81, p<0.01; whole N = 8 animals stimulated 20 min, Cohen's d = 1.80, Cliff's delta = 1.00, p<0.01; Figure 3b, c)
evidence: This is quantified from experiments shown in Figure 3b, c with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in either spontaneous contraction probability or mechanosensory response probability between 'footless' animals and whole animals.
source: Furthermore, we found no significant difference in either the spontaneous contraction probability or the mechanosensory response probability of 'footless' animals and whole animals ('footless' N = 3 animals not stimulated, spontaneous contraction probability = 0.13 ± 0.01, mean ± SEM; 'footless' N = 3 animals stimulated for 60 min, mechanosensory response probability = 0.88 ± 0.05, mean ± SEM; whole N = 3 animals not stimulated, spontaneous contraction probability = 0.15 ± 0.01, mean ± SEM; whole N = 3 animals stimulated for 60 min, mechanosensory response probability = 0.73 ± 0.07, mean ± SEM; Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c, Videos 4, 5, 10, and 11)
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of response probabilities shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c.

claim: Removal of the hypostome and tentacles ('headless' Hydra) resulted in significant changes in both mechanosensory response and spontaneous contraction bursts or pulses.
source: While the mechanosensory response in Hydra remained unaffected with the removal of the aboral nerve ring, we found that removal of the hypostome and tentacles (or 'headless' Hydra) resulted in significant changes in both the mechanosensory response and spontaneous contraction bursts or pulses
evidence: This is based on experiments with headless Hydra showing reduced response probabilities.

claim: 'Headless' Hydra still responded to mechanical stimulation with a significant increase in contraction bursts or pulses, but with lower magnitude compared to whole and 'footless' individuals.
source: When we measured the mechanosensory response in 'headless' Hydra, we found that the animals still responded to mechanical stimulation with a significant increase in their contraction bursts or pulses; however, they did so with a lower magnitude compared to whole and 'footless' individuals ('headless' N = 8 animals stimulated for 20 min, p<0.01, Cohen's d = 1.37, Cliff's delta = 1.00; Figure 3b, c)
evidence: This is quantified from experiments shown in Figure 3b, c with statistical analysis.

claim: 'Headless' Hydra responded with >2× lower probability compared to whole animals and showed >3× lower probability of spontaneous contraction bursts and pulses.
source: Specifically, the 'headless' Hydra responded with (>2×) lower probability compared to whole animals, and they also showed a (>3×) lower probability of spontaneous contraction bursts and pulses ('headless' N = 3 animals stimulated for 60 min, mechanosensory response probability = 0.29 ± 0.02, mean ± SEM; 'headless' N = 3 animals not stimulated, spontaneous contraction probability = 0.05 ± 0.01, mean ± SEM; Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c, Videos 12 and 13)
evidence: This is quantified from experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c.

claim: Longitudinally 'bisected' animals showed mechanosensory responses that were not significantly different from whole, 'headless,' or 'footless' animals.
source: We found that these longitudinally 'bisected' animals showed mechanosensory responses that were not significantly different from that of the whole, 'headless,' or 'footless' animals ('bisected' N = 3 animals stimulated for 60 min, mechanosensory response probability = 0.54 ± 0.14, mean ± SEM; Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c)
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c.

claim: The magnitude of increase in contraction bursts or pulses activity due to stimulation in 'bisected' individuals was larger than 'headless' individuals but lower than whole and 'footless' individuals.
source: However, the magnitude of increase in contraction bursts or pulses activity due to stimulation in 'bisected' individuals, though lower than whole and 'footless' individuals, was larger than 'headless' individuals ('bisected' N = 8 animals stimulated for 20 min, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 2.32, Cliff's delta = 1.0)
evidence: This is quantified with statistical analysis of effect sizes.

claim: The observations in 'headless' Hydra depended upon the types of neurons removed during the headless resection and not simply an injury response.
source: This suggests that our observations in 'headless' Hydra indeed depended upon the types of neurons removed during the headless resection and not simply an injury response
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with bisected animals that had similar tissue removal but different neuronal populations.

claim: Longitudinally 'bisected' animals had a lower probability of spontaneous contraction bursts or pulses than whole animals but higher than 'headless' animals.
source: We also found that these longitudinally 'bisected' animals had a lower probability of spontaneous contraction bursts or pulses than the whole animals but higher than 'headless' animals
evidence: This is based on comparison of spontaneous contraction probabilities across different resection conditions.

claim: The entire network needs to be intact for normal contraction bursts or pulses activity, and loss of roughly half the network leads to some reduction in contractile activity.
source: This suggests that the entire network needs to be intact for normal contraction bursts or pulses activity, and the loss of roughly half the network leads to some reduction in contractile activity ('bisected' N = 3 animals not stimulated, spontaneous contraction probability = 0.08 ± 0.02, mean ± SEM; Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c, Videos 14 and 15)
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced spontaneous activity in bisected animals.

claim: 'Body column' animals had significant reduction in both mechanosensory response and spontaneous contraction bursts and pulses relative to whole animals.
source: In 'body column' animals, we found significant reduction in both the mechanosensory response and spontaneous contraction bursts and pulses relative to whole animals
evidence: This is based on experiments with body column animals shown in Figure 3.

claim: 'Body column' animals had a mechanosensory response probability that was not different from 'headless' animals, while spontaneous contraction bursts and pulses probability was lower compared to 'headless' animals.
source: The 'body column' animals had a mechanosensory response probability that was not different from the mechanosensory response in 'headless' animals, while the spontaneous contraction bursts and pulses probability was lower compared to that of 'headless' animals ('body column' N = 3 animals stimulated for 60 min, mechanosensory response probability = 0.19 ± 0.08; 'body column' N = 3 animals not stimulated, spontaneous contraction probability = 0.02 ± 0.01 mean ± SEM; Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c)
evidence: This is quantified from experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, c.

claim: The magnitude of increase in contraction bursts and pulses with stimulation in 'body column' individuals was the lowest among all resections.
source: Although we found a significant increase in contraction bursts and pulses with stimulation as compared to spontaneous contraction bursts and pulses activity in 'body column' individuals similar to all resections, the magnitude of the increase was the lowest in 'body column' animals (even lower than 'headless' animals) ('body column' N = 6 animals stimulated for 20 min, p<0.05, Cohen's d = 1.10, Cliff's delta = 0.50; Figure 3b, c, Videos 16 and 17)
evidence: This is quantified with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3b, c.

claim: No significant increases in contraction bursts and pulses were observed over the same time period in non-stimulated animals.
source: Moreover, we did not observe significant increases in contraction bursts and pulses over the same time period (comparing activity from 0 to 20 min with activity from 20 to 40 min, see Materials and methods) in non-stimulated animals, suggesting that the higher probability of contraction bursts and pulses was in fact due to mechanical stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is shown in control experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: 'Body column' animals had a weak response to touch despite their slightly increased contraction bursts and pulses probability with mechanical stimulation.
source: Thus, based on the comparison between the probability of spontaneous contraction bursts and pulses and mechanosensory response in all resections, we found that the 'body column' animals had a weak response to touch despite their slightly increased contraction bursts and pulses probability with mechanical stimulation
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of response probabilities across all resection conditions.

claim: There are at least two independent networks of neurons based on correlation analysis.
source: We found that there were at least two independent networks of neurons based on a correlation analysis (Figure 4c)
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of single-neuron calcium activity shown in Figure 4c.

claim: One group of correlated neurons found throughout the entire body showed averaged calcium activity less than 1 s after a mechanical stimulus and spontaneous activity consistent with previously reported contraction burst (CB) neurons.
source: One group of correlated neurons found throughout the entire body showed averaged calcium activity less than 1 s after a mechanical stimulus and spontaneous activity that is consistent with previously reported contraction burst (CB) neurons (Dupre and Yuste, 2017)
evidence: This is based on analysis of calcium dynamics and comparison with previous studies.

claim: CB neurons show bursts of activity that are synchronized with muscle contractions and show calcium activity that is highly correlated with the average peduncle ROI.
source: These neurons show bursts of activity that are synchronized with muscle contractions and show calcium activity that is highly correlated with the average peduncle ROI
evidence: This is based on analysis of CB neuron activity patterns.

claim: A group of neurons near the oral end showed distinctive pattern of activity following mechanical stimulation (~10 s after), but no distinctive activity associated with spontaneous contractions.
source: One group showed a distinctive pattern of activity following mechanical stimulation, but no distinctive activity associated with spontaneous contractions. Specifically, this group of neurons near the oral end responded approximately 10 s after mechanical stimulation (Figure 4e, g)
evidence: This is based on analysis of stimulus-aligned calcium activity shown in Figure 4e, g.

claim: Putative 'mechanically responsive (MR) neurons' were found in all three Hydra analyzed.
source: We found these putative 'mechanically responsive (MR) neurons' in all three Hydra we analyzed and plot their calcium dynamics as shades of red in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2
evidence: This is based on analysis of three individual Hydra shown in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: MR neurons do not show activity associated with spontaneous contractions, indicating they are not part of the CB network.
source: The fact that these MR neurons do not show activity associated with spontaneous contractions clearly indicates that they are not a part of the CB network, but rather these two distinct networks (CB and MR) are involved in the Hydra's response to mechanical stimulation
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct activity patterns of MR neurons compared to CB neurons.

claim: MR neurons do not fire periodically as would be expected for the rhythmic potential (RP) network.
source: We also note that these MR neurons do not fire periodically as would be expected for the rhythmic potential (RP) network (Dupre and Yuste, 2017)
evidence: This is based on analysis of MR neuron firing patterns and comparison with previously characterized RP neurons.

claim: Mechanosensory and spontaneous behaviors are regulated by neural ensembles that are localized to select regions of the animal.
source: Our experiments with 'footless,' 'headless,' 'bisected,' and 'body column' animals show that mechanosensory and spontaneous behaviors are regulated by neural ensembles that are localized to select regions of the animal
evidence: This is concluded from the resection experiments showing different responses with different body regions removed.

claim: Some properties of the mechanosensory response may be evenly distributed throughout the body.
source: however, some properties of the mechanosensory response may be evenly distributed throughout the body
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that body column animals still show some response to stimulation.

claim: Localized touch produces increased calcium activity in both peduncle neurons and endodermal epitheliomuscular cells, which is associated with body contractions.
source: We demonstrate that localized touch produces an increased calcium activity in both peduncle neurons (Figure 2) and endodermal epitheliomuscular cells (Figure 3), which is associated with body contractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Badhiwala et al., 2018)
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: At least two neuronal networks (MR and CB network) with distinct neuronal activities mediate the stimulated responses.
source: We identified at least two neuronal networks (MR and CB network) with distinct neuronal activities mediating the stimulated responses (Figure 4)
evidence: This is based on single-neuron tracking and correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The CB network of neurons show fast calcium responses, and the MR neurons show slower calcium response.
source: where the CB network of neurons show fast calcium responses, and the MR neurons show slower calcium response
evidence: This is based on analysis of calcium response kinetics for different neuron types.

claim: The MR neurons, primarily found in the oral end, may consist of ec4 neurons, which are the only neuronal subtype in the oral end with an unknown function.
source: It is possible that the MR neurons, primarily found in the oral end (N = 3 Hydra), may consist of ec4 neurons, which are the only neuronal subtype in the oral end with an unknown function
evidence: This is speculated based on the location of MR neurons and known neuronal subtypes.

claim: Hydra's responsiveness depends on the stimulus intensity.
source: Hydra's responsiveness (i.e., probability of response to a mechanical stimuli) depends on the stimulus intensity (Figure 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments at different stimulus intensities shown in Figure 2.

claim: 'Headless' and 'footless' animals can still respond to mechanical stimuli despite missing an entire regional neuronal network, but 'headless' animals show reduced responsiveness.
source: Interestingly, we found that the 'headless' and 'footless' animals can still respond to mechanical stimuli despite missing an entire regional neuronal network; however, 'headless' animals show reduced responsiveness (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is based on experiments with resected animals shown in Figure 3 and supplements.

claim: 'Body column' animals missing both regional neuronal networks have the most dramatically reduced responsiveness.
source: The 'body column' animals missing both regional neuronal networks have the most dramatically reduced responsiveness
evidence: This is based on comparison of response probabilities across all resection conditions.

claim: The two neuronal networks (oral and aboral) work together and play compensatory roles in mediating the mechanosensory response.
source: suggesting that these two neuronal networks work together and play compensatory roles in mediating the mechanosensory response
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that removing either network alone has less effect than removing both.

claim: The peduncle nerve ring is not necessary for body contraction and response to mechanical stimulation.
source: Surprisingly, although the activity of the peduncle nerve ring is strongly associated with spontaneous contractions, these neurons are not necessary for body contraction and response to mechanical stimulation
evidence: This is concluded from experiments with footless animals that still respond to stimulation.

claim: The peduncle nerve ring may coordinate body contractions by enhancing the neural signal to epithelial cells.
source: One possible explanation is that this nerve ring coordinates body contractions by enhancing the neural signal to epithelial cells
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed role of the peduncle network.

claim: An additional 4 s reduction in body contraction duration in 'body column' animals compared to headless animals supports the idea that the peduncle nerve ring is involved in coordination of contractile behavior.
source: An additional 4 s reduction in body contraction duration in 'body column' animals compared to headless animals supports the idea that the peduncle nerve ring is also involved in coordination of contractile behavior (Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is based on analysis of contraction durations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Calcium activity propagates from the foot to the hypostome in whole animals during body contractions.
source: Furthermore, calcium activity propagates from the foot to the hypostome in whole animals during body contractions (Szymanski and Yuste, 2019)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: The peduncle network of neurons may be motor neurons.
source: supporting a hypothesis that the peduncle network of neurons may be motor neurons
evidence: This is hypothesized based on the propagation pattern of calcium activity.

claim: The hypostome is an integration point where sensory and motor information converge.
source: Based on these observations, we propose a simple model for sensorimotor information flow in Hydra where we consider the hypostome as an integration point where sensory and motor information converge
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Information is communicated from the hypostome to the peduncle where it is amplified for coordinated whole-body control.
source: The information is then communicated to the peduncle where it is amplified for coordinated whole-body control
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for sensorimotor information flow.

claim: There may be sufficient functional redundancy between the hypostome and peduncle regions such that removal or damage to one of them is well tolerated in Hydra.
source: There may be sufficient functional redundancy between the hypostome and peduncle regions such that removal or damage to one of them is well tolerated in Hydra
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that removing either region alone has less severe effects than removing both.

claim: The diffuse network in the body column may retain minimal processing capabilities needed for weak sensorimotor responses.
source: Moreover, the diffuse network in the body column may retain minimal processing capabilities needed for weak sensorimotor responses
evidence: This is inferred from the weak but present responses in body column animals.

claim: The fast and slow calcium responses from the CB and MR neurons support the hypothesis that Hydra have multiple, separate pathways for behavioral response.
source: The fast and slow calcium responses from the CB and MR neurons, respectively, indeed support the hypothesis that Hydra have multiple, separate pathways for behavioral response
evidence: This is concluded from the distinct temporal dynamics of different neuron types.
